blocks.x: Let me see. The first thing I want to know is your name.
My name is Linda Paz.
And we're recording this today at your home. I didn't get the address here.
The address, I'm Linda Paz. The address is 3439 New Orleans and Pleasure.
Right at Pleasure Street.
New Orleans and Pleasure.
Better get everybody's name on here who's here. Because we have a secretary types us up and she likes to get everybody's voice. Let's get your name now.
My name is Arnold Paz. I'm the oldest son of Arnold Paz Senior.
So you're Arnold Paz Jr. And how do you spell the past? D-E-P-M-L-E. Capital P and a capital D?

Yeah. Paul Aldersen. Then we have, I can give Stanselois' name in all of them. I have my daughter there. She's a Rochelle now. She was just married about a year ago. And then I have, we expect an Olivetti and she's in Detroit. Oh yeah.

This is one of my grandbabies. Oh. That's a cute picture with her hair. You see I put that little, you see I put that little ribbon up there. Oh that's cute. And that's Stanselois. Married a year today. Where was she married? Where was she married? Here? New Orleans here, right?
Right from this residence but at Pittman Church and had a beautiful wedding. She had All the wedding pictures also, some of them.
Oh, I didn't put today's date on here. This is June, what is it?
Today is the 20th.
June the 20th, 1960.
Mm-hmm. Monday.
Mm-hmm. I'm about to ask you an embarrassing question first. I wanted to get your age down here.
Yeah. Well, I'm 67. I'll be 69, January the 31st, 1961. I was born 1892.
And what's your birthday? What is your birthday exactly, the day of the month?
Well, I say January the 31st.
January the 31st?
31st of January. And only if he lived, let's see, he was 60 when he died. Died of a heart attack. Oh, I see. He was 61.
Yeah, he was 60.
And what year was it? Huh? What year was it that he died?
That was 1946. 1946.
46. 46. That's right, sir. So that was the same.
And he was insurance agent for Rhodes Insurance.
I see. And that.
So you could give Stas's name also, to speak.
Yeah, well, we could get to that, and I'm, uh, uh, uh, you could give all the kids' names.
Yeah, give all of it. Give all of it.
As it comes up in the story, it'll come up. Yeah, yeah, it'll come up. It's about a passion.
Well, now, uh, I wanted to ask you about, uh, in your own life, what's the first music you remember? Either singing or a band playing or piano or what have you?

Well, uh, we used to have, uh, piano playing. We had, uh, we had a fellow who used to play piano, go all over with us. His name was, uh, Sonny Swarm. Oh, I've heard of him. He used to play piano, you know. I have a lot of them blues. I know him when I hear him, because I heard, I hear him every once in a while, I hear him on that little radio we have. And, uh, this fellow there that's gone to California, I think, or somewhere, uh, from that great clarinet player from here. Luzanne knew him good from when she was waking up town. Oh. And he plays a lot of the pieces that, uh, we used to hear. He's a great musician. Luzanne, Luzanne, what's his name again? The clarinet player. Who's name? From around magazine. How I used to know. The fellow, no, but comes on the radio. We went to Chicago or New York or something. I know him. Yeah, the part up there, the musician, the clarinet player, you see. Not Pete Fountain.
Yeah.
Pete Fountain. Yeah, uh-huh. Pete Fountain.
We didn't get your name down.
Luzanne, D-Pez. D-Pez.
Fine.
He wants your name, you know, on there.
So the secretary, I don't know whose voice is which. Luzanne.
No. Give all of this. He'll get that out.
He'll get that out. He played a lot of the tunes you said. Pete Fountain plays a lot of the tunes that you heard in those days, huh? Yeah. And he plays plenty of them pieces.

We had a lot of them pieces he plays, you know. That was a great number. Well, Lizzie Miles sings that all the time, that song, Bill Bailey, Won't You Please Come Home. She always gets on the radio, on the television, you know, if you're seeing that. She was another one who played with, you know, sang with all of them, Lizzie Miles. And this, yeah, he played with your daddy too. What do you call this other fella? Humphrey.
Willie Humphrey. Yeah.

And the old man, you know, their daddy and all that. He all played together. Yeah. And see, we had so many of the pieces. Now this, what they call him? Not Johnny Sincere, another musician that played with James Williams. He was an old musician. He had the Armist brass band with, with, how long was it? Yes. He was a ball baller, James Williams. He was a trumpet player. He played with all them, he'd do them with some of his men. I've heard of him. He was from around Benito Street. He used to hang around James Williams. Yeah. That's what it was, around there. They'd hang around there.
And Bob Lyne, you know, he was all with them. You know, you remember Bob Lyne. I remember him. I remember him.

He died just about. He was a bass player. And sometimes he used to play something else. What did he play? Guitar? No, I don't know. I didn't know. Sometimes Bob used to play something else. And there's so many of them, I just can't remember their name. But, what do you call this man? He used to, they had the Armist brass band with the band. And, you know, you remember Bob, you remember Bob? You remember Bob?
Yeah, I remember him.

He died just about. He was a bass player. And sometimes he used to play something else. What did he play? Guitar? No, I don't know. Sometimes Bob used to play something else. And there's so many of them, I just can't remember their name. What do you call this man? He used to, they had the Armist brass band with James Williams. They played at the Lyric Theater.
That would be Robichaud probably.

Robichaud, Robichaud and then McCullin and all them played with Robichaud. Well, one time they had the brass band all together with this James Williams. And it had been so, you know, they passed off but I could picture all of them. They're all dead and gone now. He was a violin player, Robichaud. You know, you couldn't remember him. But there was a Robichaud I think that played with your dad and also played with you, eh? Robichaud, the piano player. Yeah. Well, he's still living it. Yeah, he's still living it. Yeah. Cause he, I think he played with you a couple of times.
Yeah, I played with you a few jobs. Yeah.
But he was an aged man, you know.
But he was a much younger man. That's what it is.
Well, so many of them.
Well, what about this band that had the Olympia band? Remember you used to tell the Olympia. The Olympia.

The Olympia. Well, they all had the Olympia band. Yeah, what's up from the beginning of the year? He had the Olympia band with, had the Olympia band one time with Bishy. And they had it with Jimmy Noon. And who all had it? Bishy, Jimmy Noon. Well, Uncle Richard played with, Richard McLean, he played with Olympia band. Also, Parant played with Olympia band. That's Elmer Talbot. That's Talbot. Yeah. I'm talking about, that was younger fellas, you know.
When she said Parant, you mean Talbot.

Yeah. That was Talbot, you know, Elmer Talbot. And Richard McLean, well, he's right there in the French quarters right now. We always call him, like I said Parant, because that's what he stands for. And also, that's my niece, Miss McLean, you know, husband. Well, she was a Beatrice, Oynes, she's a McLean now. And that's her son there. He showed you there. Yes, Oynes.
Oynes.
He's away now, huh? He's with, uh...
Oynes is with...

Fat Diamond on. Fat Diamond, yeah. Every night I hear him all night, you know, I'm walking back to New Orleans. Fat Diamond on the radio. He's walking back to New Orleans. And, uh, well, anyway, I was trying to think of some of that other man's...
Well, I wanted to ask you about, when you first started, you know, listening to music, you say you heard piano players like Sonny Swan?
Sonny Swan, yeah. Sonny Swan.
Did you hear any bands before you met your husband? Did you hear many bands before you met your husband?

Did you listen to music? Oh, yeah, there was... Some band came from over the river, but I can't place them. And they was a fine band, too. They was from over the river. They was with, uh, how do you call that fellow? Oh, Charlie Bokauer, the Bokauer's. Oh, I know them. Yeah, I heard them, you know. They had Peter Bokauer, Charlie Bokauer. I knew all of them. Poor, fine people. Charlie's still living.
I haven't seen him in a long time, but they tell me...

He's still living. He lost his wife. He was a personal friend of ours. He lost his wife. And, uh, then I believe some of the relatives got killed under that bridge when they was fishing. Some of them, Charlie Bokauer. You don't know Charlie Bokauer?
No, I just feed him.

He's a little short fellow, you know. And now he gave up music a long time. He used to play, uh, guitar. And he used to come home all the time and sing. And they used to make him sing that, because there was one of the girls around used to always have, uh, slippers on. And Charlie would sing a song about, uh, uh, don't send me a pose, it's shoes what I need. And, uh, Charlie Bokauer used to sing that. That was his great song on his banjo. You know, the little round banjo. You know how they had that little banjo? Charlie used to play that and sing.
And that's the kind of stuff we want. Now you strike it as great.

And, uh, don't send me, uh, don't send me roses. In shoes is what I need. That was Charlie's great song. I told Luciana, I think it was one day, uh, last week, that I'm going to try to see if I can find him, you know. He was always his sister, jolly fella, you know. And, uh, one of his sons, I think, wait where he was, Henry. He breaks that LSU. Oh, yeah. But anyway, and, uh, they had, uh, Adolph Ducanger used to play piano with him. One, uh, when he played at the Cadillac. That was a nightclub right there, Ramport.
That was his band?
Huh?
It was his band?
That was Arnold's band. You know, that was the Olympia band. And then he had Adolph Ducanger. He got killed, you know. You heard of him. Yes, well, I've heard of him.
Yes. Well, I've heard of him. I think Pete Ducanger is still alive. Oh, he ought to know. Huh? I think Pete Ducanger, the piano player, is still alive, but I haven't seen him.

Oh, yeah, I think so. But Adolph got killed, uh, he was a shoemaker. And he'd go along picking up shoes down the country, and he got killed somewhere, automobile right? You ought to remember, because that ain't been too long when Adolph got killed. You know, he was always good size. But anyway, and then he had, uh, let's see, when he played at the Cadillac, after when he took Adolph, before he had Adolph, he had, uh, George, uh, George, he went to Chicago. George, what was his name? I often hear his name called on the radio.
George.
Yeah, he passed off, I think. But he must have a son, George. George. He's not George Lewis, I think, I mean, not him. He's a piano player named George. Yeah, piano player.
George. I can't think of anybody but George E. Parker, and I don't think he went up there.
He's a George, too.
George. No, uh, uh, but George Parker did play with Daddy, but, uh, uh, uh, that's the person you're thinking of? Who? George E. Parker. You know George.
Oh, no, not George E. Parker. He never went to Chicago.

George E. Parker, he's just died not since we've been in here, because Aline told me. No, no, no. But, uh, he played with your Daddy, but not him. I'm talking about George or something. I could get his name, too, because I know different people.
Well, it'll come to you the minute we think about something else. Yeah.

It'll come to me. Well, he used to play piano there at Cadillac. My Uncle played, uh, uh, Uncle Dave sometime used to play, Dave Depass used to play clarinet. Well, that's my husband's brother. He used to play sometime with your Daddy, you know. Jimmy Newman was playing there also one time at the Cadillac. Until he went away and we had that cook auction with him. And, uh, they used to play at the fairgrounds, you see. They had the Armist brass band at the fairgrounds. And they had the young Olympians who were supposed to be at a jazz band, you know, play all that bratty music that's fast stuff, you know. And the nice people would dance by the Armist brass band. You'd have to do that skipping dance, you know, like waltzing around and all that. But your Daddy would play it in other words, what they called the Tunk. They'd play out there. And, uh, sometimes, like, my friend and I, we'd go looking around and your Daddy would say, Don't come here, baby. Get away from here. You know, it wasn't for the nice people. For the rough and ready ones. They'd play that. Your Daddy would have that hat on and the uniform, you know. And he used to wear, like, suspenders, you know. And when you get real warm there and beating that drum, he'd put one of them suspenders down, you know. One of the suspenders down and he'd have that cap on the side. And I'm telling you, he really could beat that drum, too. Could make one of the best, how do you call that, rolls on the drum, you know. A lot of people say he really had a gift to that, you know. He played by air, too, but he really had a gift to it. Because often, different people say you'd never think that, you know, that he played. And he had so many opportunities to go away, but he never would accept it. Because I never would want to go away. I always wanted to stay, you know. And he always wanted to say, come on, let's sell out and go away. And when Manuel Perez went away, still a long time, you know. You know Manuel Perez, the trumpet player. Well, then after a number of years, he came, stood here and laid down and died there. He had a son. Is his son still playing?
Manuel Perez's son?
Perez had a son.
I've never heard of his son.
Yeah, he had a son.
That's funny, I didn't know about that.

He had a son who was trying to follow his footstep. I don't know if he ever kept it up, you know. Well, he was a fine musician, you know. He was, Manuel Perez also was with, one time, they had, let's see, what was the name of his band? The Superior? I think the old one. Manuel Perez? The old one. Was it the Superior?
No, that was Billy Morrero's band. Billy Moran's band. The Imperial, yes. It must have been the Onward band, you think?
No.
The Imperial?

No, the Imperial, yeah. Imperial, that was his dance band. Yeah, he had the Imperial, that's right. That was his dance band. The Onward was a brass band. I knew it was something about, he had the Imperial. Cause, and sometime he played with Papa Sellers, then. Sometime, you know, cause they both were trumpet players, but sometime, yeah, I played with them.
I wanted to ask you what year you got married in.
Oh, that was 1913. 1913.
Yeah. Had you known your husband a long time before that?
Yeah, he come up with my brothers, you know.
I see.

Yeah, he came up with my brothers. And my brother and them used to play ball together, and he was, uh, uh, worked with the the class, as a hard carrier, you know. Then, uh, then he, uh, uh, drive a wagon and sold charcoal. And then he was, uh, he worked, uh, about, uh, about 10 or 15 years for Parker Davis and Blake. He was, uh, he was driving, uh, with his old truck, there was a wagon, you know, at that time. And I believe that's, uh, that's the last place he worked. Till after when World War I came along, well then, had to go work for the government. Well then, during that time, he was playing at Cadillac also. And he wasn't getting but, uh, $25 a week. And making a wonderful collection, as much as $19 a piece at night, you know, collection. And, uh, he had, uh, a little can he had picked up, you know. And, uh, they had that tissue paper, you know. And they had a little kitty on there. So often I say, there's something now about the kitty, you know. Well, I believe one of the first ones to come out with that when he had a dog and them with him. And he took that, uh, little picture of the kitty off of that paper. And he glued it on the can. And every time they'd be playing the dances at the Cadillac, they'd play a lot of them jignet dance, you know. Yeah. And swapping the partners, he'd tell me how they do, you know. You know, the man would tap you on the back and you'd have to turn loose the lid and sit fast. You know, the guys had to play fast. And every time he'd say, and the money was flushing. And he'd holler, feed the kitty. Feed the kitty. And he'd say, that little can would just get so full. You know, and that's how they made barrels of money like that. They made, that man's made money worth nothing but collection. The salary was $25, but the collection was so good. Now, I remember one time, well, the children was all unborn and the baby was just about a couple of weeks. When during the time he was playing in the French quarters for Petone, for the Papa. They used to call him the Papa. And then they played for Petone. You know, he was, he was, award boss. Well, who was the mama? Well, that was some other man they played under, some fellow. Some, that was the name they used to call him the mama. Another big fellow that was out at Lanassus. That was at Lanassus. They made plenty of money there too. That was during World War I. When they played for Tony, you know how much they was getting a night? A dollar a night. A dollar a night. And Petone used to come in and there was more fellows looking to get those jobs. It was really hard to get, but they'd make little collections. But a dollar a night from eight to four. Eight to four dollar a night. And I remember your daddy would stop right there in the French quarters and buy his capro bread. He liked it, you know, with them seeds all over them, you know. And come home with the rest and his little collection. And that used to go a long way, you know, because all that he was collecting insurance in between them times. And oh, it was just so much to think about it. And he had another great clarinet player. We was the only one who had a radio during that time. And Lou Armstrong used to come on, like I said, once in a while. But when Lou Armstrong was up there, you know, off the line and we'd get on the radio. But most everybody in town would be saying, I'll be at your house, I know tonight Lou is going to play, you know. And this boy, he lost his mind. He was great. Henry Julian. You heard of him?
I have, yes. But I can't appreciate it.
He was a saxophone player and a clandering. Henry Julian. He was great. Really great.
When was his time? What was his best days?

Well, he, let's see, he was about his age to be now. I mean, well, he would maybe be about in his fifties now. In his early fifties, you know. He would be about Henry Julian, you know. And he was, oh, great musician, you know. But he lost his mind. And he had, that was some of his relation, this little fellow. He's still playing, eh? Live around the parlor or somewhere. Let's see. Oh. He's a little bit of...
What instrument does he play?
Oh, you call him, he's a little...
Saxophone, apparently. This young fellow? Oh, oh, oh.
I was a young fellow. He wouldn't be too young. He would be about... Maybe he's older than Crump. Oh, yes.
I've heard of him. What was he, uh?
Frank Crump.
He was a saxophonist.
A little bit of a fellow. Well, that was Henry Julian's, uh, brother-in-law. I think he used to play on that saxophone, eh?
Oh, I think Didi told me about Henry Julian. I believe Didi mentioned him one time. Oh, yeah.
Didi is blind, you know. Who? Didi.
Didi is blind, the trumpet player.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah.

Oh, he is another great, uh, trumpet player. Well, he played with Arnold a lot of times, too, yeah. I know him personally, you know. Yeah. He had asked me to send you over to take some lessons for him. Yeah, well... He was living out there on Galveston, that route, eh?
Yeah.

He's still there. His wife is also a piano player. He's another personal friend of ours. It's just naturally when people are getting older, you know, they lose track of each other, you know. And I used to get out in the street every day and go to church, and every now and then I'd meet a lot of people I knew so good, you know. The children say, oh, mama, yeah, she'd go out, know so-and-so, you know, and all that.
Say, mom, what about the, uh, some of that stuff about the Lions Club and some of that stuff, you know?

Yeah, well, we had the Lions Club. Yeah. Well, we had the Olympic band then at the Lions Club. Well, that was also, uh, Talbot was in there then. And in other words, everybody knew him, like, call him Cuckoo. They knew Talbot by that means. And, uh, he used to sing, uh, Louis Armstrong's song a lot, and everybody really thought, sometimes people in the dance would say, uh, Louis Armstrong sang, uh, about, uh, if you be my baby, uh, the Butter and Eggman, you know? Mm-hmm. That song?
I want a big Butter and Eggman.

Yeah. Come be my, no, I'll be, uh, Butter and Eggman. Well, two, three people used to think, he was saying that so good, Talbot, you know, which was Cuckoo. He, uh, a lot of people would come to us and say, that's the Butter and Eggman? So we'd say, yeah, that's the Butter and Eggman. And he used to go around advertising trucks, you know, in our trucks, uh, them furniture waves. When he was gonna have a dance like at the Lions Club or Santa Centers. Well, most times they'd have two bands. They'd have René, you know, Kid René at the Santa Centers. Well, Kid René played, uh, trumpet. And his brother played, uh, Joe René played, uh, drum. You know. And, uh, Richard was, and I'd swap over, I think he was with Kid René there one time. But, uh. He was, yeah.
He told me he was, yes. Yeah.
McLean. Yeah, McLean.
When he was playing banjo then.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. Well, honestly.
I want to ask you how your husband got started, uh, playing drums.

Well, he started, uh, he told me he used to take two sticks, you know, drumsticks. And his mother had one of them wooden bits. And that's how he started beating drums on the back of the bed. And he used to say, I know, put them sticks down. His mother would get after him by putting the sticks down. And that's how he started playing drums. Beating on the back of his mother's bed. And then after that, well, when he started out with the drums, then he got the drums. That's when he was working with Parker Davis, when he got the drums. And then he got together. Louis Armstrong was in the home, I think. Yeah. Louis Armstrong was in the home, and they used to, now and then, René Clue was in there one time. And all that. Well, all of them used to come out, you know, and they, they was quite young, all children. And then they started up the band. And, uh, he had his brother with him. Day of the past, you know. And, uh, that's why I'll tell you, well, during that time, you'd get along, and they had, off and on, they'd have Bechet. Well, they had to bring him there and keep him there all day, you know. He was a very good fella and smart, but they really had to look him up because he wasn't reliable. And if you wanted to play a job tonight, well, you had to get him there and keep him all day. Because he'd blow you up. If somebody stopped him, he'd sure blow you up, you know. But he was a great musician. And, uh, and then also during that time, when they first started with the band, you had Joe Oliver. He was a yard boy, somewhere around Magazine and St. Mears. All even told me the people's names, but I forgot. And I heard something about Joe Oliver. Uh, when, uh, we was in the project. They was asking different people and we sent in to, uh, who was it? Uh, out there in the French Quarters. Oh, I can't get that fella's name. He had interviewed, uh, Lizzie Moran and, uh, he was talking about the history of, uh, of Joe Oliver and all them different bands. So I made my girl write a letter to the station that I had a picture of Joe Oliver and all that. And I would like to, like, get in touch with his wife and I would let her have it, you know, or something like that. But we never got the answer. We never got no answer for the picture. Because I didn't mind to say give him up, because maybe if I could get a little copy of him or something, just to have him. But I'd be glad to give him, almost, you know, all the information, you know. And he looks fine in there. He looks swell. That picture I have. I'm going to get it to show you. Yeah, Dr. Savings. And, uh, oh, so many of them boys all used to go along and they could pick him up somebody and make something out of him right away and put him in a band. I remember one time when the bands was hard to get. He sent some fellas out with them little, uh, with some other good mans that could play, uh, lead the band. He sent them out with a, how do you call that? A Zuzu? A Zuzu. Them little Zuzuz. He sent them out with them. That was one of them, then?
Yeah. But didn't Byron make these first games with the Zuzu?

Oh, yeah. I hope to tell you. He played good with that. He played good with that. He could play that good. And your Uncle Rudolph went out to play. Your Uncle Rudolph had a little wooden box he made him, about a big like that, covered up with black, uh, with black calico and tack all around with brass, uh, tacks. And he got a little bit of, like a little Christmas horn, and went out and played big job for that. The people clap him and ask him back. What was his name? My, uh, brother-in-law, uh, that's my husband's brother, but, uh, Rudolph? Uh, Rudolph Boye. He's out there on Moray Street. Oh, no. Annette Street, he lived. He also, he's playing. Of course, he's been kind of sick. And, but, uh, he's still playing. Excuse me. He's still playing. Rudolph Boye. He belongs to that union. You know, your Uncle. Well, he had a little, uh, a little horn. He had got a little Christmas horn. And he used to go play jobs with that. With Parade with the little Zuzu. They'd play. And your daddy gave, uh, Uncle Richard gave my brother, Uncle Al, my brother Alfred, some, uh, get banjo lessons for about a week, and they'd send him out on a job. When they'd be scrapping up, they'd make, and everybody would always be well satisfied. He'd split the band, you know. And, uh, that's before all that union business. Well, they didn't have all that, you know. And then they could dictate them days, uh, if they didn't want to be in the union, because sometimes they used to laugh, say, that fellow, what's his name? He had some sons. He was the first one started with all that union. And sometimes he'd come, your daddy and all, they'd be playing, and here he'd come. Knock him off. I know you've got to get in the union. He'd say, oh man, get away from here. Let me play. And, uh, they wouldn't play, and they wouldn't have to play. They wouldn't have no union at that, you know. You know. You know. You know. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

He went away, didn't he? He went to California. Oh yeah. That's right, I heard that. Because I saw him about six or seven years ago, because he worked on that clan's house, you know, and all so on. You know, Mr. John. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
And then the time he got home, he was supposed to be in good health.
He didn't like to play parades after Walter Blue died?
Yeah.
Did that scare your husband?
Yeah.
Did that scare your husband when Walter Blue died?

No, I said he never did like it. And after Walter Blue died, Walter's voice. No, he didn't ever believe in walking a lot, like that playing parades. And them days was different. After, of course, like now the union's behind those fellas. But them days, you had to go and play with a man. He wants to go out this way because he wants to pass by maybe some of his girlfriend's house. You had to make a big round and go around the other way. And you'd have to play overtime. And now they don't allow that, you see, playing that overtime and all that. So them days it was different. And he played them. And men's played for the balls. A couple of years ago, Tommy and Daddy, that was from 8 to 4 in the morning. From 8 to 4, that man's playing.
8 to 4.
8 to 4. And they had no... They cut out all that...
24 hours, man. I'm ready.

You know what they cut out... And look, they used to play long tunes. It wasn't like y'all now. And they cut out all them quadrilles. They had quadrilles and large ones. And getting ready to have that quadrille. That was fun. Because if a man knew how to dance, he showed himself then. And when they'd holler, they'd holler almost like the chicken. And they'd holler, swing your partner. Swing your partner. Swing your partner. Swing your partner. They'd holler, swing your partner. And you know how they do for the quadrilles. And they'd holler, grab your partner. And the man would grab the lady and swing out. Then they'd say, swing your partner. And the man would come and cut out his steps all in front. You know the lady. And she'd be making her motions too. And that was good. And they'd hand their hand. And they'd say, chain. Chain something. Some boy. And they had the ladies and men. Everybody catch their hands together. And they'd be going, oh, that was really grand. You know why they cut it out? Your daddy said, because it was so long, the people would give the ball. After they realized a number of years after that, they was losing money. Because them days, people would give balls. And every time bands stopped playing, well, the gentlemen would take the lady to get refreshment or supper. And when I was going to the ball, it wasn't like y'all heard about. I don't have nothing to eat. We had turkey, ham, and gumbo, and all that. 40 cents for a nice turkey dinner. The young ladies didn't drink no beer. It would be a disgrace if somebody would go tell your parents to see you getting a beer in the ball. Ladies didn't go around. You know, not no young ladies. Maybe the elder women would go up in there. And you had very few to do that. But more so, the pops, you'd have pop. And I wouldn't say it was punch. It was lemonade, you know. But you would really get that something to eat, though. They'd treat you to that. And when they'd have the... Some of the gals would hardly... I just loved to dance so much, I didn't care about nothing to eat. I mean, we'd take a pop. But if the band would... And they'd strike up, hit the foot, and then ta-ta, ta-ta. And then when the band would get ready to strike, you'd see everybody, if they're going to have the quartile, they'd blow the horn, you know, to give you the... See if they're going to have the quartile. And you'd be looking for your party, you know, who could dance that, you know.
What kind of tune was that play, ma?

Like what? I just can't think of it now, see. But... I saw my names, you know. Yeah, Dad, I mean Uncle Arthur and Cousin Walt and Bob, and he was a handsome-looking fellow. And they had very small... You know, and they could make all the motions, and I mean, they're making that step. The numbers used to be real fast.
Fast numbers, huh? What?

For the quartile? Yeah. Certain times, depending what, you know, certain things. But the walls, when you had to walk, you know, it wasn't. Not all of them was fast. And they had, they had, they played a mazooka. They had a waltz, and they had shatters. They all don't play that. They all don't have no shatters. You know how the shatters was. They make so many steps, and the ladies put this out a little bit, and the man waltz around. The shatters was beautiful. They have it, what you call them? Murray, Murray has them shatters and everything. Arthur Murray can dance them. Arthur Murray can dance them shatters. I mean to tell you, he really dances them waltzes and everything. That man can dance. And you see them shatters on there, alright. They're still doing it some places. Cousin Leona does that. Cousin Leona.
Oh yeah, she still does that. Every year. Oh yeah, she still does that.

Oh she knows who I was doing. I gave a lot of dances in life, and I gave a lot of lawn parters. And I made pretty good on them, you know. And I think, I wouldn't say if I was a little younger, I could really, now I could understand giving them, but I just wouldn't have anybody to go in with me, you know, to give them, you know. And you really had such a different opportunity. I don't know, the people was a lot different in some respects. And then you'd get a police, you could choose the police you want at the door, you could tell them which one you wanted to send. And you'd give people them days, big friends, you know, they had personal friends and everything, you know. And you could tell them what police to send you, to be at the door and all that kind of stuff. And they really made money, you know, selling tickets and all that. They made a lot of money. I gave a lot of game parties, you know, lawn parties. Everybody would come with game dresses, you know. And I had several times where I would all be playing for somebody else, where I'd have to get another band. I had a little fellow. The last dance I gave back, Taunty Street, a lawn party. The fellow would play it. I had Charlie, a blind Charlie, who was a piano player. And he could play. A blind fellow. You wouldn't think it would be blind. A lot of people used to kid and go on, because they wouldn't say Charlie was blind. They'd pass seeing him nailing a picket on his fence and all that. And you could tell the time, you know. He was great. They had really some great musicians a long time ago. And they really had a gift to that, you know. And it was, I don't know, it was plenty different. So it is, I don't say the youngsters ain't great today. They're really great. And, but them old time musicians, they're really good players. For instance, I could take Celestine and all that. Oh, they're really good players. And you know, often I wonder. I remember seeing Celestine about, I saw somebody, I saw Celestine about a year before he died. And do you know that Celestine was playing when I was a little child, about 10 years old. And he looked the same until he laid down and died from when I was 10 years old. I remember he used to come to Slidell and play for us with Manuel and them. He'd have two trumpets, you know. Manuel played a lot of times with him. And they had, what did I say, the superior.
Imperial was my name.

Imperial, yeah, the imperial. And used to give constructs over there and balls, you know, in Slidell. And what you call them, Celestine would come out there and everything. And the man, I was about 10 years old. And Yaron got to be a, of course, he's been dead a couple of years. But he really held out good. And he wanted me to let you come to him and take some lessons. He had offered to give you lessons, you know, free of charge, you know. When we lived on libertarian. Quite a few offers, you know. He had plenty of opportunities, you know, with great musicians, of course. Oh, like the fast pitch, you know. Because I'll play with him a lot, you know. Oh, all the pitch, you know. You see what all used to play with Celestine? Well, he was doing that time at the Cadillac and he had two drums. He used to leave one at the Cadillac. And then John Morero used to play a guitar with him. And so he was sent his drum by John and he'd keep on at the Cadillac. So John said, but I know, how do you know if your wife's going to be home? Oh, she's always home. She don't go anywhere. So when John come up with it, he said, I know I'll say you was going to be home, Mr. Pass. I said, yeah, but I'm going to fool him one of these days. I said, he's always sending somebody home. I said, go home. My wife's always home. So I said, one day he's going to come and be mistaken and I'll be gone, you know. So sure enough, John comes to bring the drum. He had two sets. He used to leave one at the Cadillac and then when he'd go play a picnic, then he'd have that other. And you know what you call him? That was another great musician. How about with Dodd? He was a handsome fellow, too. That drum player, Oylos Trepanion.
Oh, yes.

Yeah. Oylos played a lot of times in his job. You know, at night, he would come ass on to go play. You know, sometime, one time I think he was playing at that about three times a week. And he used to go play in Oylos Trepanion's place, you know, sometimes. I don't remember him, eh? So...
Where were you born? I wanted to ask you about that.

Right here in New Orleans. Right here on Taunty between Tulane and the street coming this way. I think it's... Banks? Banks. And the house was just as good as if it was just built some years ago. You know, often I pass and I look at it, you know.
Your husband was from that same neighborhood?

No, he was from around here. Not around here, but around... Around... Around... Prairie Street. Around... Around Caloret, Laperouse. And then when he was small and his mother was living and all, they lived back Olyan and... Olyan and... Olyan and... Olyan and... Russia Blade. Olyan and Russia Blade, yeah. They lived around there. But he'd come up right in the... He'd come up after that, when the time he started the band and all that, right there in the Tramie. You know, right in the Tramie. That was the best part of his life. He was raised all in the Tramie. When Bishan and all of them used to come to the house, they was right in the Tramie by his aunt. You know, by Loretta's mom. Right there. His mother died, he was very young, you know. And he was raised by his aunt. And she left a couple of sons, but the rest of them... They had him and his sister, and a brother was the past, and the rest was Boye. Now, during that time when they had... Uncle Tom used to play with... Also played music with Sam Morgan and them, you know. Was that the bass player? No, that was my brother-in-law. He was a guitar player. What was his name?
Octave Boye.

Octave Boye. Well, he played for a couple of years, you know. He didn't keep it up. But most of the way he went to play, your daddy would recommend him to go... You know, when people would ask. Well, the most of the way he went through his life playing music, and everybody addressed him always as the past. You know, your daddy would send him, they knew he was the brother, and he'd never take it and explain him. Just Uncle Rudolph would after. Good many years, well, he'd put out his name, Boye, you see. But most of the way your daddy sent him in jobs. Oh, you just get so many jobs, you know. And sometimes he'd split the band, and of course, if he had to take somebody else that maybe wasn't a professional, well, he'd take some of the good men and put them with the man that was a professional. That's how he split the band, you know. Just after a number of years, well, after the union, you know, they didn't go for all that. But he really could master that band. He learned to be a manager under Jimmy Moreira. Jimmy. Billy was the old man. And Simon's dad.
Billy was the old man.

Yeah, Billy Moreira. Billy, that's right. And there's Eddie and Lawrence and Simon. Billy learned him to be a manager. Billy learned him. Because often, I would have had some of them contracts to show you, because I used to still keep them, still keep them. Well, it really got away after. Instead of cheering, my oldest girl, she'd just get along some things, and she'd say, Mama, what do you want this? This is junk. I had contracts that I used to sign. Say, for instance, they play a ball for Carnival tonight. Well, they'd sign that ball for next Carnival right away. The fellow who didn't get them that night said, I'll be at your house in such a time. You know, for deposit. And he always kept a big roll of money home, deposit. You know. And he played a lot for a fellow over in Greenville, Mississippi. I've forgotten that man's name. That man used to come here all the time and hire him. Take him and that man there, Santiago. And about, did you ever know about little Boynell Santiago? Yeah, he was right on it. Yeah, when he played, best of the time, he played with Arnold too, you know, Boynell did. There was another one of those gift-comer fellows, you know. He had another little brother that he died. I forgot what was his name.
Well, Lester still plays, that brother. Huh? Lester Santiago still plays. Oh, yeah. Black, huh?
Yeah.
Black.
Black said he ain't. Oh, yeah, it was Boynell died. Black is the one, you know. Black is still playing. And that's his brother-in-law, Picky, you know.
Oh, yes, I know him and Chani.

Yeah, married one of, oh, he's married one of black sisters, you know. Picky did. Well, anyway, now that was all a little bit of children growing up in front of us, you know. And his mama was a good friend with Arnold and a lot of his sisters, Gertrude and all their visits our house, you know. They was big friends with us all. And it's just to say how that family, you know, naturally people passing off, you know. And the younger generation, a lot of them don't do like, see the children of Santiago and different other people like when we was coming up north. If we knew a family, well, we'd visit that family. But you get the young generation today, and lots of their relatives, they don't look around, you know what I mean, and keep up like that with the families. Now, what our family were like, there were a lot of them passing off. But, well, my brothers was all living when they had a family reunion, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve. Well, all I'd find in my house was just crowded, you know. But all that changes things, you know. Make sure you forget a lot, you know.
Oh, the machine was off when we were talking about Black Benny. What did he play, Black Benny?
Oh, he was a drum player.
Did he play the snares or the bass drum or both of these?

He played, he played, he played a bass drum and then he had them little, what you call them, tambourines that hit on, they played that too. Then he had them sags you hit on the drum, you know, like little brooms, you know. He played that. He was a great musician, you know. And we went to a cornerstone laying in Covent that Benny played. The whole band played that. And Bueller's mother had, Church had given it as a National Academy. But I just went because we knew them so good. But anyway, and Benny played that for that cornerstone laying out there in Covent. We caught the train right here at, by the terminal station. You know what was that? And Sunday morning. Oh, they had so many of the excursions, you know, was plagued with plenty of people, you know. And that night he came back, that woman stabbed him that night in the heart. Oh, and the doctors worked so faithful on him and he was well-taught of. And he lived three days, he was trying to make. And I still had kept that piece out the paper, you know, and that got away from me. I used to always, right now I got to write some more papers there. But, uh, Lucy Ann hardly does me that. But my oldest girl, she'd get to cleaning up things. And I guess she about to throw them contracts away. Because I always meant to keep some of them contracts, you know. I used to, he done saw some of them contracts. Yeah, I saw them contracts. It was big like that. When all you sign up, you know, the contracts for dates for different jobs, you know. And it was so nice. I always liked, had liked to keep those kind of things. They'd look over them, you know, to know just what was what and how to go at something, you know, and all that. But anyway, to come back to Benny, it was really sad to see. Because he played a lot of them, he played all them parades. He had liked that, you know, and he played all them funerals. He used to have so much second hand lying behind them funerals, you know. Until after a while, the priest was, I was at our church where we was living across from Peter Claven. Well, that's how I said, I never want to live across by our church no more. Because every time you look out there, you see a funeral coming with a band of music. People be crying. And then after you get to looking at the funeral, you didn't have any courage to do any kind of work. And it just kept you upset all day. And I used to say, I didn't want to live near a graveyard no more, you know, a church to see how the funeral. When we came to see for this place, I wasn't so much looking at the place. So when we made up our mind about the place, I told my children, I said, I never want to live next to a church or across from a graveyard. And now I'm going across from a graveyard. All them little men across the street in that yard, I thought that was tombs. And they said, Mama, graveyard? There ain't no graveyard around there. I said, for sure. So sure enough, there's this, them little men, she's got all, how you call them, I'm getting a script for the bow. And he's got all a little men here. And I gave one look and I thought, sure, we was moving across from a graveyard.
Well, the Catholic people used to have bands with them too? I see that's how I remember.

Well, yeah, Father St. Lawrence and Father Moron, they cut that out. Oh, I can't understand. It was terrible. The second line was so bad. And then it got so on the last, it had police, you know, to keep in with a funeral. That was terrible. Well, most of it was different people from what wasn't, you know, like, they had a few, maybe like the refined people and maybe that would be the family's request, you know. See, when Pa Rea died, plenty of people wanted to know, indeed. They didn't want no funeral. After they have the funeral, they play the marsh. Poor Sam Morgan, he's dead and gone. He's the one who started that, toying that marsh. And now they play that for a dance. When the saints come marching by, Sam Morgan made that up and toying that up, you know, to a jazz piece, to dance. And the second line used to come and bang, they play it. Didn't he ramble? He rambled till the butcher cut him down. You know, that's after they buried a man. And then what else did they play? Something else did they play. And then the priest, you know, to such terrible second line, they cut it out. The man wouldn't be at what, it's just man, you know, they buried me. They had one woman uptown, some Miss Cole. They buried her with two bands of me. Uncle Rudolph went to see that. But I never, I heard of it, but I didn't see it, you know.
She had all those long parties.
Yeah, she was a spiritual, too, you know. What was it, Third and Willow?
Yeah.

And she was the woman that they say used to insure so many people, and then they caught on to her, and they would die right now. She had that lawn place up there. It was on Willow, wasn't it? Yeah, I think it was somewhere back there. How do you call them? Miss Cole, her name was Miss Cole, and she had that big place on the corner of Willow and some of them street back Magnolia or something. I don't know the streets much, you know. I know how to get to them, but I hardly ever keep them in mind, too.
Kid Bunch tells me about that.

Yeah, they had a lot of the bands used to, you know, all the bands used to go in there and play. Of course, she made plenty of money, that woman, but there was different kind of people from the people down here. They always select, you know, the Creole people. And of course, I was a different set. We'd more like go to espionage, you know, just to see, to find out something. We wouldn't go into maybe a dance. My brother used to take me anywhere, and I'd take a good look, sis, and we'd look around and see. We'd just walk in there like overseas and walk out. We'd just like to go and see, you know. I'd like my children to do that right now, go see some things just to know. It's always good to know, you know. And she raised plenty of money on that place, you know. Yes, indeed. Well, you see them kind of jobs where your daddy didn't go for that too much. Them kind would pull them tanky people. He was one man, he liked a different one. I said, who was that? He ain't no fighter. Well, he sure wasn't a fighter, you know. Like they told Uncle Chum that time, he said, go stop that fight. Chum, one of my nephews, you know, been in a place for years, a bartender, and he called him Chum, you know. And he said, go stop that fight. And they just put that on the paper because they figured his wife was jealous, you know. And he said he wasn't a fighting man, he was a lover man. But he said, no, no. He didn't say that. And I know my nephew didn't say that because he's very timid and very, you know, refined. He wouldn't want us to maybe, and I read it. And they said, and I know he didn't say that, but his wife is jealous, you see. And they said it done that to make her jealous, you know. They put it in the paper? Yeah. They said they told him to go stop the fight and say he wasn't no fighting man, he was a lover man. Big headline on the Louisiana week that they had that on the paper. And that was his, so anyhow, their daddy was, I don't guess he ever had any fights when he was a little child or something. He said Uncle Rudolph is like that, Uncle Todd used to like to fight Nick, and Uncle Dave wouldn't date nothing. But Uncle Rudolph and your dad, it was, they all, everybody, the family always put them select, you know. They was different.
Oh, about Ms. Cole, you said she had some kind of insurance business?

You know, she had, they say she used to insure so many people. And so she didn't insure them, they died. So that got so now that somehow or another like that, they say they didn't want her, you know, they stopped. That's how, I think she was the cause, they said they made that law that, you couldn't put nobody in the insurance less than their son. Because people used to go along and put you in the insurance, they'd go put anybody in the insurance, then let corporations come and bury you, you know.
And you didn't even know they would put you in the insurance?
No, that's how you could put people a long time ago.
No, it didn't. You could collect the money yourself.

You can't do that now. Yes, indeed. You could put anybody in the insurance. So long you just paid it. And more so, well, they got some of them now, the doctors don't see them, you know, or something. But you could put there, a lot of people put sick people in the insurance, you know. Yes, indeed. You didn't have to let a person know, but now you put a child in there, unless they're very small. But your own children got a sign to put their self in the insurance. And then if you have them paid a policy you want to draw, you can't, if you're paying the money, you can't draw it, you got to get them to sign. Remember, I had to draw a policy off of you when you first come out of the service? And I had to send my daughter away at his house to sign, so he could sign. You can't get that money. Well, it's changed now.

It's definitely changed now. Yeah, it's different now. Oh, well, how did those funerals work in the olden times? Who would pay for the ban? The what? Who would pay the ban at a funeral in the olden times?

Oh, well, lots of times they made a collection for that. Say, for instance, if the fellow was a man that was well known and had a lot of friends, and a lot of times the club paid for it. But if it was just a simple fellow that was just what you call one of those, I guess maybe you say a ladies man, I don't know. Popular amongst the ladies, I don't know what it meant. Maybe if he was a big gambler and he had nothing behind him, he'd have one of the greatest funerals out and make a collection. People would pay, and some people them times would go pay for people without asking the parents permission, the family permission, and even stop that. They'd make money if they want to get flowers. Oh, and people would be giving big money for that. They'd cut all that out. They're on to people for that. You know, a lot of people that even didn't know. But they're still making...
Yeah. They're still passing the sake off, huh?

Oh, yeah. Make collections and people be giving a couple of... But I mean, the majority of the people is catching on to all that now, you see. Because say for instance, ourself, if we want to give something, we'd all give nothing like that. We wouldn't... and nobody wouldn't come and ask, of course, to count people. We know it's different. We always send, you know. But I mean, you get some of those people would die maybe like... Tank. Tank and a baby. Yeah. They made collections for that for them.

And he was laid out in the Caledonia. Yeah, I've seen a picture of that. And the Caledonia tank. Do you remember the tank? Yeah. I remember. And the man at the Caledonia said, he sure wish they could hold him over about two more days. Because he sold out everything. Yeah, I saw that. Caledonia, St. Claude, St. Philip. They had the wine bottles and everything. Yeah, he was laid out in there.

Yeah, he was a lottery vendor. And he was a nice fellow to win. He liked that liquor, but he was very respectful. You know, I treat all the people very nice with a lot of respect, you know. And nobody had no trouble with him, you know. But he asked if I knew him. I hope to tell you. Many times he brought me my money. I played lottery and he brought me money in a big piece of newspaper. Two sheets of the newspaper was money I'd win from tanker to lottery. It was a lottery vendor.
Oh, so you used to be pretty lucky with lottery. You used to win a lot of the time. Yes, indeed. When I was at Penn, they used to sell vengeance pebbles.

All them days was common. You'd say that was good days. You used a lottery vendor. There wasn't as much going on like you had. You had so much going on now. Look, they had lottery. How many times when my husband's eyes got bad? And he was working, but not as much, you know. And it was time of depression. Well, like when my children would need something, I'd just get out there. My brother-in-law used to kid and say, Lynn, they ain't got no, God ain't in no lottery. I said, well, he sure answers my prayer. And I'd tell my children to get ready. And all the vendors knew me good, you know. And the children would just go there and make them sign to come in. They'd go by Hartmire, build all the way they say. They'd never seen children like that. Just out their brain. And they'd say, what do you want? I said, play the famous ones. And you didn't have to tell them which was the famous. And the children, I said, y'all want, if they want shoes or... Look at that, they must got some of that stuff on them. First time I'd seen them, I'd been in the front. And I said, um... Tell them about that. Did get ready. Huh?
Wait a minute, it's about to run off again, you know. All right.
Marie Laveau, you was back there in them days. Oh.
And the children would get ready. Mm-hmm .
The last one I remember, this little fella got killed.
You remember this fella, Moran?

Wait ma. Oh, excuse me. And the police shot this little guy. Then it all happened in this area around the Calzone. Get him, Lou. They even have a club they call the original Second Liners. I don't know if you noticed when they have a band, a guy called it with Banner. And they're supposed to be some of the greatest Second Liners in the world around here. Like Snow, Govins, Bull Weaver, you know, guys like that. I've been to them since I was a kid. Well, they pass the cigar box and they go to all the places in the neighborhood, like the grocery store, the bar, all the people that's got a little business, the knock on doors, people without a dime, quarter. I mean, they just go all over the Trimm A section. Well, the Trimm A section covers that area from about, say, from about Orleans to Esplanade, from Clavin to Rambo, or maybe to Burgundy. And they just pass the box and everybody put the money in. And then they hired a band. And the union has made a special provision or something for funerals where the guys actually pay a little cheap. You know, they more or less, they don't really get a top salary, you know, for playing this thing. So after they're raising money, they just hire the band. And the Second Liners be out there, and they, well, I guess you've probably seen them. They go through all the motions, just like if the guys, their brother, you know, when they're taking them to the church. They're crying, got their heads down until they turn their body loose. Well, after they turn their body loose. Well, I tell you, a guy explained to me the whole significance behind the whole thing is this. In other words, I mean, it makes a little sense if you look at it like this. They say when a man dies, the idea came from, well, I mean, he's dead, and that's it. I mean, that's the way they figure, you see. And after, they never take the body all the way to the graveyard because it's too far. You know, they always walk, say, maybe a little distance. And then after they get there, they give the body all the respect in the world. You know, they let the body get about five blocks away, and then the band strikes out. You know, da-da-da-da, they're ready to roll. And that guy hit the bass drum. You know how they do it. Boom, boom, boom. Oh, man. And I mean, if you're standing in the street, the best thing for you to do is to get out the way because they might just dance over you. You know what I mean? So that's the whole thing. But they believe that that guy, he's on his way. I mean, now let's have fun. You know, it's all over. But a lot of people be under the wrong impression. I've heard different people talk that didn't know. They think that they play this music while the church and all that's going on, but they actually play hymns and funeral marches and all that. And they walk in a slow, slow temple, you know. Like, it takes them an hour to get rid of the body. They walk so slow. And everybody's real. They got their heads bowed and everything else. They really, you know, do it up in the right way. But when they leave that body, that's the end of it.
Well, look, according to the Bible, that's the right thing to do.

Well, I mean, that's what I'm saying. It's got some meaning behind it, you know. That's the whole meaning about it. They don't go on and moan for days. I mean, it's over. He's gone. Now let's go back to living again.
Where do you think the custom came from?

Well, no I don't. But I've heard at times that they did that in France at one time, but maybe they did it in a different way. Like, I figured from what I've heard, I mean, it's not a fact, but just like during the time I was in the service, we played perfumes, but it was done in a real solemn way, you know, pious. Everybody's, the drums is all in black and everything, you know, like that. Well, maybe they had that idea in France, when the people came to this country, they just thought of putting a band with it, but they did it a little different way. They swung, you know.
I said, you ever heard of Bab Frank's band?
A little bit, but not enough. Not much about Bab Frank.
Well, I knew him personally. I don't know too much about his band, but he's daughter, maybe, but that's Ann Buell's daddy, you know. Bad Frank.
And what is her name now?
He used to play, huh?
What is her name now?

Well, her name is Miss Augustine. Buell Augustine? Meek is Augustine, yeah. Buell Augustine. She lived right out there on La Perru Street. But we are, let's see, I think, she's March. She's just, she's a few months, she's a few months younger than I am. But I don't think I could send her there unless I see her, and maybe she could impress her mind. But she had poor memory. And we came up together, and she, I don't remember nothing too much. Ann Buell, sweet. I was telling the gentleman, I don't think I could, I have to see her and ask her if she remember anything about her daddy. Oh, yeah. He used to play a piccolo. Yeah. Ann Buell's daddy, he was good on that too. But I said, Ann Buell has her memories very full. And she's three months younger than I am.

Ann Buell, well, tell me this, ma. She's been kind of sick with that stroke and all that. Did you ever listen to jazz bands doing all this? Like a father, when they were, guys would come out of my house when I was a kid, they would go. You know, instead of knocking on the door, they always did that. And a lot of people do that now.
Who is that?
You know, she can send it. You know that thing they had, that whistle? Oh, yeah. And you always know those are musicians. Did you ever find anything about her?
I had the trumpet players do it on parade, but I don't know where.
But why do you think they do it on parade?
I would guess to get everybody ready to play the piece. Yeah.

You see, and then, too, there were bands, I've seen guys play like that. There were bands where the guy knew so little about music. I think this is kind of the part, you know, that I bring this out. Of course, I found this out when I was a kid. He knew so little about music until he couldn't tell you he was playing in the G. Well, if I played a tune and I said, well, man, Tiger Ray, B flat, well, he couldn't do that. And he'd blow that piece on the horn to establish the key. And everybody would listen real close. And then he'd know what key was in it. You see? Well, how I first found it out, I was playing on a job with an old fella. And somebody, well, you know, we was playing some old tunes. And somebody asked for Melancholy, baby. You know, the team Melancholy, baby. So I knew it, and the piano player, he was a little old town. And the guy asked, I asked him what key he played in that. Well, he said he didn't know. So he played, you know, a few balls of it, and then he went from the fifth to the time. That's where he was good at. And the guy told me, that's the key. He said, he couldn't tell me the key. So now that the guys are law and law, that's, I don't think they do it now for that. It's just a tradition. Did they want some ice? Now they're just passing on down. Some ice? But right now.
We have plenty of fresh milk by then. Want a glass of milk? Oh, no.
This water's fine. I want this.
You know what I mean? Yeah, I'm a party man.
I don't have anything good tonight. Got it.
Didn't know.

And I've heard trumpet players play a tune, and they had a high. Well, that came from the old days too. When the dance is really swinging or the party or whatever they're playing, and they get, they had a part of their howl, and the band, not really howl, but the guy is running and saying, all right, everybody for themselves. And then the guys be playing, they're going to be, and he said, band out. You know, well, that's when they're going to swing and really strike that groove, you know. And he's swinging. And then the band is swinging. So after the band finishes the tune, and the people clapping, they look like, you know, they're crazy about the tune, and the guy is doing it again. He's going to go. And I have seen bands that did that three times, and every time they pick it up in a different key. Because the guy doesn't know his horn. But he can play it. Man, he can play you anything. But what happened, he didn't know his horn. And when he would pick that same tune over again, he did it in another key. And everybody followed him. And I mean, if you know the thing about music, man, that's kind of amazing. Yeah, it is. You know? He knew something if he could do that. Well, he had terrific ears, and that's what most all the guys back there had. They could hear everything.
Oh, I wanted to ask you about the Magnolia Band. Do you remember the Magnolia Band?

Yeah, I do remember something about them. I believe, that's what I was telling you. I think that night I gave that lawn party, I think that was the Magnolia Band I had. I was trying to think of some of the fellas' names, but there was a fella that played trumpet there, he had one leg. And I can't place it. I know old Richie would maybe know who it is. They played a lawn party for me, you know. He had one leg.
Do you remember Pops Foster and Willie Foster? Pops Foster's George Foster, he played the bass?
Oh yeah, I remember them.
And Willie played the guitar?

We used to call him Troste. We used to go, bands used to have were hoistels them days at people's house and they'd invite you. You know, we had plenty of that ourselves. And this fella, we went to a lot of things. I don't know what band he had here. Did he die in California? Did he die in California? Yeah, Aura. Yeah, Aura had a band here. Used to call it Aura's Band, Aura's Brass Band. He was a trombone player. Well, they had a couple of brothers to play music. They come from right up around, somewhere around Coliseum Street, all around up in there, Coliseum and Cades. It's just been so long, I forgot. What about Piku?
Eh? Piku, you know Piku, huh? Piku. He's right there, over there, Robinson Street.
Yeah, the horn around. Still blowing his horn. That's why he's living. And he drinks like Samson. Oh man, Piku. Did he play with your husband? Oh! Oh! Oh!
Sorry, that was one of them main friends.

Piku. Piku made a... They made... When all of them was playing at the Lions Club. People who met when all of them was playing at the Lions Club, every time the club started going down, and Lopez was the president. And when all of them get through playing, Lopez said, you'd be packing to him. Lopez said, when you come to Pam, it didn't make no money. So Piku got together with all of them and said he was going to compose a song, sing it for yourself. And so Piku made a song. If you ever meet him, he'll tell you that. They all got together and every time you look all in Cuckoo, which was tabbed, they'd come home and Piku and Thomas Copeland. You remember Thomas Copeland?
The bass player?

I've heard of him. Well, he was with the IZL, you know. They was all with the band then. Thomas Copeland, IZL, Arnold, Piku, and sometimes they used to use Moran, Jimmy Moran. The bass player? The old man. Oh, Moran, the trumpet player.
Oh, her.
Yeah, Horvath, that's right. Horvath Moran. Because they got the other brother. I forgot his name. McGee.
Morris Moran played drums. Oh, yeah. But he's aware.
He died. He died at sea.
He was shipped out. Oh, yeah.

You know who that is? You know, Moran's brother, he married one of them girls and their relationship to them Barbarans. Well, they know how to tell you. How to do it. So, Piku told all of them they thought everybody was writing music. So, Piku, they got together and they made a song. They was going to name it, See For Yourself. Every time they get through playing music, poor Aolo piece would come. And you say, well, I know. You see for yourself. We didn't have a crowd. We didn't make nothing. So, they said they were going to name the song, See For Yourself. So, every time you look, they're coming home, playing, playing, and over and over, over and over, over and over. So, finally, they got it straight. And they sent it to get it, or where to get it done. To Washington. And that was the last of that. They don't know if Piku got anything or what. That was the last to see for yourself. We haven't seen Piku ask them, say, what's the come of that song you all had composed? See for your coming. And see what he'll tell you if he remembered. He's right there. He's got a bar room now.
What about four or five times? Didn't y'all have some story behind that?
Somehow I heard somebody. Four or five times a baby's story.
Yeah, I heard that. I can't play in school.

I can't play in school. But Piku's got that bar room there on Ursuline and Robbins. He always did drink, you know, to the extreme. And he's still drinking, you know. Then got older. I don't think he played. He plays in there. He plays his famous piece. He plays always. You know, in that ballroom, he'd be playing when he wanted to draw a crowd. . .
I was going to ask you about guys like Chris Kelly. Did your husband ever play with Chris Kelly? Oh, yeah.

Yeah, I remember him. Yeah, I hope to tell you. It was all kind of like right hand vows. You know, they had a certain bunch like Chris Kelly and all them boys. They're like, this was right together. Whenever you want them, all of them, you go right there, Parita and Ramport. They used to get all their jobs from right there, Parita and Ramport, signing up. Everybody come in town. That's where their headquarters was.
That ego's the line, huh?
They made plenty of money then. And poor Bob Lyon. Bob Lyon was a great musician. He was a fine bass player.
Well, what about Buddy Petit? What kind of trumpet player was he? Buddy Petit?
He played trumpet.
Did he play with your husband?

Oh, yeah, all of them. Buddy Petit was great, too. He was a good player. He had a funeral when he died. You know Armstrong came in, especially with him. He had a big funeral. Buddy Petit, oh, that was all... He was another fellow who drank hard, but he played. You could say he died young. And, oh, that was the boys really playing. They made money. All the boys made money. And I saw the boys in them days, I don't know, just... I think pick up that instrument. You know, they're self. They really are... I don't think there were a lot of them. Wasn't much like Reed as well. Like Bonnie, you know, Big Eye. Well, he was all right, too. But he started quite down. He was playing with Arnold and him. He was about 14 years old. He used to come practice home, you know. Roy's home. And then after he went away, you know. Arnold's... I think... Arnold was the first... The Olympia band was the first band ever played. Colored band played at the auditorium. Arnold, the Olympia band. I'm sorry, I couldn't hear you.
Where did you play? I said...

He was my husband's band. It was the first band, colored band, played at the auditorium. Oh, I see. That was the... During a carnival. He was hired by... It's so hard, we were in between, I just stopped up. He was hired by Walter Hubbard. You know, he used to work for all them people, you know, that had to call for parades. And... Paran. I said Uncle Richard. And... Thomas Copeland. Izel and all that. And I believe he had that boy, Moran Whitton, that time. And after he played there, that's where Duke Ellington came in and played there. There was the second band played at the auditorium. Your daddy was the first one. Played at that auditorium. What's happened to Thomas Copeland? And all that, none of that, never what, never right, none of that. What happened to Thomas Copeland? Well, he died, you know. No, I didn't know. Yeah, he took very sick. And he lost, his wife went down in a canal in an automobile, you know. And that car made a fake on him. And he took sick from that. And then he had, he was at the hospital and they say he had broke a bottle or something. And tried to commit suicide, cut his wrist. But he got all right a little bit. He never was so, you remember him. Yeah. But he was saying how he was so glad to meet you, you know. And... Cause you met him somewhere you was playing, I think. Yeah. And so anyhow, he got come all right. And then after that he died. He used to wait for the slaughterhouse. Yeah. But he killed all them cattle, you know. That's the cattle.
Was he about your husband's age?

Who, Thomas Copeland? Yeah. I think he might have been a little younger, no. He might have been a little younger, you know. Not too much. I think Izel, you know, we used to call him Ogoose. I think he was about in his age, you know. Maybe he was a little old, I don't know. Maybe just his belt or something, you know. But, uh, there was all, there was all with the band. He'd give that up a good while ago, this fellow Izel Robinson. And he was like, what we call Ogoose, you know. I saw him. Cause he had a, I think he had a stroke and thing. He had been right sick. He had given up a good volume. But anyway, to tell you, uh, by all them playing there, you never heard nothing of that, you know. And when he put that little write up for my niece's husband in there. Well, I don't know who gave that record. Cause, uh, they didn't mention too much at all was the foundation of him playing. Cause he did all bodies first horn and everything. And he was the one that started them out. And Richard also first started out with, he played a little bit, but not too much with no band. Cause all first took him when he had Sidney Daysby in. Sidney Daysby in was his trumpet player. He died not too long, you know. Cause at least send me words, you know. Sidney Daysby. Was he still playing in California?
No, I think he had a restaurant out there. Oh yeah.

Well anyway, he, uh, was our neighbor one time. He owned a little house right down St. Philip. But, uh, I don't know why, but, uh, I guess all got kind of disgusted when that man, I'll never forget that. The associate, uh, do so much about it. Not even like in a, a praise, you know, he didn't put nothing about it or nothing. And he'd get right smarter pictures. After that, somebody else had came through and said, you know, that, uh, he could get the pictures back. But he didn't know, I don't know. He gave a lot of pictures he had at home, but different boys, you know. Sidney Vinn, I don't know if you knew Sidney Vinn. I've heard of him.
The Climbing player. The Climbing player. He got killed. Well that's Warren Bell, that's Warren Bell's uncle. You tell me about that.

Cause his daughter had asked me if I had his picture, you know. And all, but I didn't have none of them. I had this Matoya fella. You ever heard of Matoya? Oh no, Matoya. He was great, you know. And, uh, we had picture of Pierron and all that. Now he was a fine violin player. And I think a little while before he died, uh, we had read of them or he told all somebody's stories about it. It was very expensive, I think. He was great cause he played out there, uh, I'll tell you that. West End or something. I could have just, was during the place I guess, if I'd pass on there. But, um, what Pierron used to play, you know. He was a little fella, had one, one leg short and the other. You remember him?
I never saw him, but I know plenty of people worked with him.
He had a little foot, you know, and it kind of, was short and wet up, you know. But a fine little fella, fine musician.
Well when did Thomas Copeland die? I forgot to ask you what year he died.
Oh. Let's see. He died, uh, before Pierron, you don't remember?
He died recently.
He died recently, um, I mean, uh, uh, because I remember a little bit of that.
After he died, Anstasie must know.
He died after Pierron.
Yeah. He died of a stroke.
Yeah, because, uh, he died after Pierron.
Around 50.
He must, if he died after Pierron, he must have died in 47 or 48. He died after that day. No, Pierron died in 50.
50, yeah.
No, he didn't die after Pierron.
He died, he died around 47.

He died before, because you know why we was uptown when he died, because. That's right. That's right. And he took Sanzington away. Right. And he said, uh, friends, uh, where he worked at made him, uh, uh, design of a base. You know, old flowers. Yeah, I remember when I was coming back now.
I was coming back now. To the top of the score.
Because he had loved that base. Yeah, he could play it too.
He could play that base too.

Yeah. He was a fine fellow. You know what I mean by that, uh, he was very respectable. He really was nice. Very nice. Very nice. But, uh, he just fretted about his wife going down in that canal, you know. That really grieved him. Never was the same out of the way.
Did I ask you if you knew a trumpet player named Guzi or something like that? Guzi or Guzi or something like that? Yeah.
Maybe. Maybe. That name kind of sounds familiar.
What about, uh, Zoo Robertson? Do you remember him?
I know that name too.
He was a trombone player years ago. He was down.

He was so much musicians. Oh, yeah. There used to be plenty them days. They don't be, look like the posts they have, but you don't hear musicians like them, do you? Look like everybody you knew them days was a musicians. Most everybody look like you knew of, you know. Yeah. Everybody wanted to play and all that, be musicians. That's why I tell you, uh, we tell my children that when we went out to different houses, went out to our friends' house, moved from one house to the other, like time of Kings Day and all that, we brought our own piano player with us and we all would get out there and try to sing. They used to say I was a good baritone and all that. We'd all try to do something. Didn't all try that.
What tunes would you sing in those days? Eh? What tunes would you sing in those days?
Well, there's, what tunes?
It's what we're naming some of the songs.

Oh, the songs? Oh, well. Well, it was old songs already, but anyhow, I used to sing them. Uh, When You Were Sweet Sixteen and Oh You Beautiful Dog. And so many of them, because nine days they laughed, because I don't know. Nine days I hung some songs. Did you ever hear any Creole songs then?
People sing Creole songs?

Well, uh, no more, but just, uh, like if the band would be playing and sing that El Aba, you know, and say some things in Creole like that, you know. And, uh, like sometimes, uh, well, just say a few words and make, more so make, just the scales, uh, them French songs, you know. My daddy's sister used to come be singing French and we'd just go behind, you know, and she's, like . and doing all that, you know, and, ah, singing them French songs. I was telling the children the other day, when my dad's sister would come home, they'd be so warm, and she said, oh, I'm so warm, I don't know what to do. And she'd have to take her waist off, and stay, but I know where the dog be in the dam. I said, well, today they have to sleep, because she would be glad for that. Say what?
Parade used to sing Hail Our Bile.

Oh, yeah. Parade sang that to Orade and the Shewitt, didn't know what to do, and all the cheering, you know who used to sing that to? That other fellow, he was a great saxophone player, I think he's still living. Bruce Lough? What's his name? Bruce Lough? He's our dog, too, I think.
Bruce Lough? Bruce Lough?
Oh, Adolf, he had a stroke.
Alexander?
Yeah. Tat. Tat. You're talking about Tat.
He had a stroke. He has glasses.
He was a brown skin, short brown skin.
Yeah.

But you know the last time I saw him? You know the last time I saw him? At a birthday party when he gave four little coffee on the couch. He had a stroke. He had a very little sick. He played a bass, what you call him? Baratone. Saxophone, man. Yeah. Yeah. He was great. Yeah, he was supposed to be one of those. He used to be with Arnold all the time, always played with him. He was a fine fellow. Oh, there's so many of my guests eventually come to you.
Oh, what happened to that fellow who used to live on Prayer and Demand? He used to play with Dad.
Prayer what?
Rugello. Remember Rugello?
Bruiser?
Rugello.
I don't know. Rugello? Because there's some nicknames. Rugello, you remember?
Yeah. Rugello.
You remember on Demand?
The man in Prayer, he was living right next to that stage.
Oh, yeah. Sure. He was a little saxophone player. Saxophone, kind of thing. Oh, yeah. And I think he used to be a whole lot with D.D.
Yeah, he used to play when he put playing on his phone.

I think he lived somewhere back there yet. The man in Prayer, on the same side with that oil station there. Right. He got married. He married some girl from Lake Charles, I think. And he wasn't married no time. I think she died a harder time. And then I think he married somebody else and did die. He's a very nice guy. I think he lost his mother and everything.
You say, did he play with your... Who's that? Did he play with your husband too?

Did he? Oh, yeah. Played at some of them nightclubs together. Because I just can't play this thing. I played at the bungalow. He played at the roadhouse. He played out there. For the Cadillac. At the Cadillac. He played for that man that we called the Marmalade. It was one of them big nightclubs out there by the French market. That one had to live for me. At Lannasa. Lannasa's place. Because cousin Walter worked there. Walter Bell worked there during that time. He was chef there. that was another place you got

segments.summary: She recalls piano player Sonny Swan and radio clarinetists, mentions Lizzie Miles and Willie Humphrey playing with her husband, and James Williams.

segments.title: Who played in the Olympia band: Noone, Richard McLean, Talbot

segments.chapter: Early music and the Olympia band

segments.title: The Cadillac nightclub band: Adolph Ducanger and the pianist George

segments.chapter: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
segments.title: Marriage in 1913; husband's jobs, Cadillac pay, the kitty can, wartime wages and radio

segments.chapter: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
segments.title: Henry Julian and Frank Crump
segments.summary: Discussion of saxophonist Henry Julian, who lost his mind, and his relative Frank Crump.

segments.chapter: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
segments.title: Didi, the blind trumpeter

segments.summary: Olympia band at the Lions Club, Talbot singing Butter and Egg Man, bands at the Santa Centers with Kid Rene and Richard McLean.

segments.chapter: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
segments.title: The zuzu horn, Uncle Rudolph and early union days
segments.summary: Early makeshift bands with a zuzu horn, Rudolph Boye, splitting the band on jobs, and an organizer who forced musicians into the union.

segments.summary: Description of the quadrille, why it was dropped, ball suppers, and the dances of her youth.

segments.summary: She gave lawn parties and dances, hired a blind pianist, and recalls Celestin playing in Slidell when she was ten.

segments.title: Celestin, the Imperial and her husband's two drum sets
segments.summary: Celestin and Manuel Perez's Imperial at Slidell, her husband keeping a drum at the Cadillac, John Marrero, and drummer Oylos Trepagnier.

segments.title: Where she and her husband were born and raised
segments.summary: She was born on Tonti Street; her husband was raised by an aunt in the Tremé after his mother died.

segments.title: Octave Boye, Billy Marrero and her husband as band manager
segments.summary: Her husband sent family and others on jobs, learned managing from Billy Marrero, signed contracts and played for a Greenville, Mississippi, man.

segments.title: Playing the lottery in the Depression

segments.title: Bab Frank and his daughter Ann Buell Augustine
segments.summary: Bab Frank, a piccolo player, and his daughter, who lives on La Peyrouse Street.

segments.title: The musicians' whistle at the door and on parade

segments.title: First black band at the auditorium; Copeland, Izel and Desvigne
